Practice tracker
A simple way to visualize optimism practice in your app is to mirror this “Optimism Practice Tracker” structure (4 logical tabs). You don’t have to expose it as a spreadsheet, but you can use the same fields in your UI.

1. Daily Log (core screen)
Purpose: One quick daily check‑in that feeds everything else.
Fields to capture per day:
	•	Day 
	•	Date 
	•	Optimism Rating (1–10) 
	•	Main Situation Today 
	•	Dominant Narrative (Optimistic / Pessimistic / Mixed) 
	•	Small Win Action (what they did) 
	•	Small Win Outcome (how it went) 
	•	Optimism Skill Used (dropdown from skills menu) 
	•	Barrier Noticed (dropdown from barriers list) 
	•	One Thing I Can Influence (today) 
	•	Notes (optional) 
Visualization ideas:
	•	Line or sparkline of Optimism Rating over time. 
	•	Icons for which skill was used (for example, 1% More Possible, Small Good Thing Hunt). 
	•	Tag chips for barriers (Defensive Pessimism, Negativity Bias, etc.). 
[6seconds]​

2. Barriers Map (psychoeducation + personalization)
Purpose: Turn abstract barriers into a personalized map.
Rows (each row = one barrier):
	•	Barrier Type (Defensive Pessimism, Negativity Bias, Fear of Naivety/Social Judgment, Cultural/Family Norms, Learned Helplessness, Other) 
	•	Description (My words) 
	•	Internal/External 
	•	Related Journey Phase (Phase 3, Phase 4, etc.) 
	•	How It Shows Up (thoughts/behaviors) 
	•	New Reframe or Response 
	•	Support/Skill That Helps 
In the app:
	•	Show each barrier as a card. 
	•	Allow user to fill “How it shows up for me” and “What I’ll try when this shows up.” 
	•	When they log a barrier in the Daily Log, you can hyperlink back to this card. 
[6seconds]​

3. Skills Menu (optimism toolbox)
Purpose: Make optimism skills explicit and selectable so users can see what they’re using.
Columns:
	•	Skill Category (Fast Optimism Hit, Explanatory Style, Future Orientation, Small Wins, Values, Relapse Plan) 
	•	Specific Skill Name (for example, “1% More Possible,” “Small Good Thing Hunt,” “Temporary vs. Permanent”) 
	•	Day/Phase Introduced (reference back to the journey) 
	•	When To Use It (simple heuristics) 
	•	My Example (user’s own example) 
	•	Helps Me How? (user’s perceived effect) 
In the app:
	•	Present as a Skills Library with tags and “favourite” icons. 
	•	When they select “Optimism Skill Used” in the Daily Log, pull from this menu. 
	•	Show usage frequency per skill (for example, “You use 1% More Possible most often”). 
[6seconds]​

4. Weekly Summary (coaching view)
Purpose: Give a 7‑day reflection for patterning.
Fields per week:
	•	Week # 
	•	Start Date / End Date 
	•	Average Optimism Rating 
	•	Top 3 Small Wins (free text or bullet list) 
	•	Most Used Skill (auto from Daily Log) 
	•	Most Common Barrier (auto from Daily Log) 
	•	Biggest Shift This Week (user reflection) 
In the app:
	•	Show a weekly card with: 
	•	Average optimism (number + color band) 
	•	One “Most used skill” badge 
	•	One “Most common barrier” badge 
	•	A text box for “Biggest shift” they can fill at the end of the week. 
[6seconds]​

If you want, I can now:
	•	Convert this structure into exact on‑screen copy for each area (field labels, helper text, tooltips), or 
	•	Help you prioritize a “v1” with just Daily Log + Skills Menu and add Barriers/Weekly Summary later.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 1
fields.teaching_content:
Effective verbal expression often starts with one clear point per message, not three.
	•	Prompt Think of a recent conversation. Write: “Underneath everything, the main thing I wanted to say was…”
	•	If–Then If I find several “main things,” I’ll circle the most important one.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 2
fields.teaching_content:
Vague words confuse; specific words land.
	•	Prompt Rewrite: “This is stressful” into something more specific (e.g., “I feel overwhelmed by the deadlines and unclear priorities”).
	•	If–Then If I struggle, I’ll add “because…” and finish that sentence.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 3
fields.teaching_content:
Long sentences weaken impact; short ones are easier to follow.
	•	Prompt Take something you’ve said recently and rewrite it as one sentence you can say in a calm breath.
	•	If–Then If I keep adding clauses, I’ll ask, “What’s really essential here?”
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 4
fields.teaching_content:
“I” statements share your experience without blaming (“I feel… when… because…”).
	•	Prompt Turn “You never listen” into an “I” statement that fits your life (e.g., “I feel dismissed when I’m interrupted because it seems like my ideas don’t matter.”).
	•	If–Then If it sounds long, I’ll keep just one feeling and one behavior.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 5
fields.teaching_content:
Clear verbal expression includes naming feelings, not just thoughts.
	•	Prompt Complete: “Right now, what I think is…” and “What I feel is…” about one situation.
	•	If–Then If I’m not sure what I feel, I’ll pick the closest word and allow it to be approximate.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 6
fields.teaching_content:
Good communicators can say, “I don’t know yet,” without collapsing.
	•	Prompt Write a sentence you’d be willing to say: “I don’t know the answer yet, but I can…” (e.g., think about it, get more info, get back to you).
	•	If–Then If I feel pressure to perform, I’ll remind myself this sentence builds credibility.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 7
fields.teaching_content:
Many conversations drift because there’s no clear ask at the end.
	•	Prompt Take a vague request and rewrite it: “Could you please _ by _ so that _?”
	•	If–Then If I feel needy, I’ll reframe clarity as respect for both of us.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 8
fields.teaching_content:
A 1‑second pause can turn reactive blurts into thoughtful speech.
	•	Prompt Draft one “pause phrase” you can use (e.g., “Give me a second to think about that.”).
	•	If–Then If silence feels awkward, I’ll remember it often reads as thoughtfulness.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 9
fields.teaching_content:
Phrases like “You always…” or “You just want…” claim to know others’ motives.
	•	Prompt Turn one mind‑reading phrase into an observation: “You just want to make me look bad” → “When you said X in that meeting, I felt embarrassed and wondered how I came across.”
	•	If–Then If I hear “always/never” in my head, I’ll rewrite it as a specific example.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 10
fields.teaching_content:
You’re beginning to make your speech simpler, truer, and more specific.
	•	Prompt Complete: “If my words were 10% clearer and kinder, my relationships or work would change by…”
	•	If–Then If I’m not sure, I’ll guess one small improvement I’d like to see.

Days 11–20 – Active Listening as Part of Verbal Expression
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 11
fields.teaching_content:
Good verbal expression starts with what you say, but also when you say it—after listening.
	•	Prompt Think of a time you jumped in fast. Write: “If I had listened a bit longer, I might have heard that they were…”
	•	If–Then If I can’t tell, I’ll mark this as an area to watch in real time.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 12
fields.teaching_content:
Paraphrasing shows you heard and lets them correct you: “What I’m hearing is…”
	•	Prompt Draft a one‑sentence paraphrase you could say to someone right now (real or imagined).
	•	If–Then If it sounds stiff, I’ll tweak the wording until it sounds like me.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 13
fields.teaching_content:
Asking a clarifying question prevents talking past each other.
	•	Prompt Write two go‑to questions, like “When you say X, what do you mean?” or “Can you give me an example?”
	•	If–Then If I assume I already get it, I’ll still ask once this week and see what I learn.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 14
fields.teaching_content:
Reflect both what they said and how they seem to feel: “You’re saying X, and you sound…”
	•	Prompt Draft: “So the main thing is , and it seems like you’re feeling about it.”
	•	If–Then If I’m wrong, I’ll invite correction: “Did I get that right?”
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 15
fields.teaching_content:
Letting someone finish a thought before you respond changes how your words land.
	•	Prompt Complete: “Today, with one person, I’ll practice not interrupting and will wait until they fully pause before I speak.”
	•	If–Then If I slip, I’ll notice it and try again instead of giving up.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 16
fields.teaching_content:
Behind most speech is a need: to be heard, to be safe, to be respected.
	•	Prompt Think of a recent complaint. Write: “Under those words, I think the need was for…”
	•	If–Then If I’m not sure, I’ll try naming 2–3 possible needs.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 17
fields.teaching_content:
Small verbal cues (“mm‑hmm,” “I see,” “go on”) show you’re present.
	•	Prompt List 3 short phrases you can say while listening that feel natural to you.
	•	If–Then If I tend to go completely silent, I’ll consciously sprinkle these in.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 18
fields.teaching_content:
Owning it can rebuild trust (“I realized I wasn’t fully listening earlier…”).
	•	Prompt Draft a 1–2 sentence repair you could use the next time you zone out and need to circle back.
	•	If–Then If this feels embarrassing, I’ll remind myself repair beats pretending.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 19
fields.teaching_content:
Healthy conversations share airtime; you don’t have to dominate or disappear.
	•	Prompt Complete: “Most of the time, I talk _ (more/less/about the same) as others.” Then: “In one relationship, I want to slightly shift toward…”
	•	If–Then If I don’t know, I’ll ask a trusted person for their perception.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 20
fields.teaching_content:
Your spoken words get more effective as your listening improves.
	•	Prompt Write 3–5 lines starting: “When I slow down and really listen before I talk, I notice that…”
	•	If–Then If I haven’t tried it much yet, I’ll describe what I expect will change.

Days 21–30 – Emotional Dynamics in Verbal Expression
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 21
fields.teaching_content:
People hear tone at least as loudly as words. Calm words in a sharp tone still land as sharp.
	•	Prompt Recall a recent tense conversation. Write: “My words were saying _, but my tone was…”
	•	If–Then If I’m unsure, I’ll imagine how they might have experienced it.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 22
fields.teaching_content:
Naming how you feel reduces hidden tension: “I’m feeling nervous as I say this.”
	•	Prompt Choose a safe context. Draft: “As I share this, I feel…” and fill in one honest emotion word.
	•	If–Then If it feels too vulnerable, I’ll practice first in writing.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 23
fields.teaching_content:
Attuned speakers check, “How is this landing for you?”
	•	Prompt Draft a question you can ask mid‑conversation: “I’ve said a lot—how is this coming across?”
	•	If–Then If I fear the answer, I’ll remind myself that clarity helps me adjust.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 24
fields.teaching_content:
Stating your intention can soften the impact of hard truths.
	•	Prompt Draft: “My intention in saying this is…” (e.g., clarity, care, problem‑solving, not attack).
	•	If–Then If I notice my actual intention is mixed, I’ll be honest with myself before I speak.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 25
fields.teaching_content:
Sharing feelings is healthy; dumping them all on someone without consent is not.
	•	Prompt Draft a consent check: “I’d like to share something I’m upset about—do you have space for that right now?”
	•	If–Then If I worry they’ll say no, I’ll remember a small “no” now can prevent a bigger rupture later.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 26
fields.teaching_content:
You can soften edges without erasing your message: “This is hard to say, and it’s important.”
	•	Prompt Write one softening phrase you could use before a blunt truth.
	•	If–Then If I tend to sugarcoat too much, I’ll keep the truth intact after the softener.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 27
fields.teaching_content:
Sometimes questions are really about reassurance or safety, not just information.
	•	Prompt Recall a loaded question (e.g., “Are you mad at me?”). Write: “The emotion under that question might be…” and “I could respond by saying…”
	•	If–Then If I usually answer only the surface question, I’ll consider addressing the emotion too.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 28
fields.teaching_content:
Flagging importance can signal others to listen more carefully.
	•	Prompt Draft one sentence: “This is important to me because…” that you could use in real life.
	•	If–Then If I’m afraid of sounding dramatic, I’ll remember people can’t read importance without clues.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 29
fields.teaching_content:
Verbal skill includes cleaning up when you’ve spoken in a way you regret.
	•	Prompt Draft: “I don’t like how I said that earlier. What I meant to say was…”
	•	If–Then If I feel defensive, I’ll focus on my behavior, not theirs.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 30
fields.teaching_content:
You’re learning to speak in ways that fit the emotional moment, not cut across it.
	•	Prompt Write 3–5 lines: “When I pay attention to emotion in a conversation, my words change because…”
	•	If–Then If I’m still learning, I’ll describe one adjustment I want to keep practicing.

Days 31–40 – Audience Flexibility
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 31
fields.teaching_content:
Good speakers adjust language, pace, and detail to the listener.
	•	Prompt Pick two people (e.g., a peer and a senior leader). Write: “To talk well with _, I need to be more…” (e.g., direct, detailed, patient).
	•	If–Then If that feels like “fake,” I’ll reframe it as kindness and translation.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 32
fields.teaching_content:
Jargon excludes; simple language invites.
	•	Prompt Take a complex idea and explain it in one or two plain sentences as if to a new employee or teenager.
	•	If–Then If it still sounds technical, I’ll try removing acronyms and fancy words.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 33
fields.teaching_content:
Some people need slower, spaced‑out speech; others prefer concise speed.
	•	Prompt Think of someone who looks lost when you talk. Write: “With them, I could slow down by…”
	•	If–Then If slowing down feels unnatural, I’ll experiment in just one conversation.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 34
fields.teaching_content:
Instead of guessing, you can ask: “Do you want the short version or the detailed one?”
	•	Prompt Draft that question in your own words.
	•	If–Then If I worry they’ll say “short,” I’ll remember I can always offer detail if they ask.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 35
fields.teaching_content:
Light mirroring (formality, directness) can make people feel more at ease.
	•	Prompt Choose a person. Write: “Their style is more _ (formal/casual/direct/story‑driven). One thing I can mirror is…”
	•	If–Then If I feel like I’m losing myself, I’ll mirror only one small element.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 36
fields.teaching_content:
Culture shapes what counts as respectful, rude, or warm in speech.
	•	Prompt Complete: “One cultural norm I’ve learned about around communication is…” and “How I can honor that is…”
	•	If–Then If I don’t know much, I’ll see this as a cue for more learning.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 37
fields.teaching_content:
When someone is stressed or upset, they can process less information.
	•	Prompt Write: “When someone is maxed out, I can adjust by…” (e.g., saying less, slowing down, focusing on one point).
	•	If–Then If I tend to overload, I’ll commit to one key sentence in those moments.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 38
fields.teaching_content:
Before diving in, ask: “Do you want advice, a sounding board, or just someone to listen?”
	•	Prompt Draft that question in a way you’d actually say it.
	•	If–Then If it feels corny, I’ll test it and notice their reaction.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 39
fields.teaching_content:
“Does that make sense?” is okay; “What are you taking away from this?” is better.
	•	Prompt Draft: “Before we wrap, what are you taking away from this?”
	•	If–Then If I’m afraid to ask, I’ll remember misunderstandings are worse later.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 40
fields.teaching_content:
You’re learning to tailor your voice rather than using one default setting.
	•	Prompt Write 3–5 lines: “When I adjust my style to the person or group, I notice that…”
	•	If–Then If I haven’t tried much yet, I’ll describe one adjustment I’ll test next.

Days 41–50 – Difficult Conversations and Boundaries
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 41
fields.teaching_content:
Dancing around hard topics confuses everyone.
	•	Prompt Pick one tough topic. Complete: “The simple sentence that says what this is about is: ‘I want to talk about…’”
	•	If–Then If that feels too blunt, I’ll pair it with a kind preface later—but keep the sentence true.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 42
fields.teaching_content:
“You’re careless” attacks; “When X happened, Y was impacted” describes.
	•	Prompt Rewrite a criticism into an impact statement: “When _ happened, the impact was _.”
	•	If–Then If I slip into labels, I’ll rewrite them as behaviors.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 43
fields.teaching_content:
Boundaries need clear words, not just hints: “I’m not okay with…”
	•	Prompt Draft a respectful boundary sentence for a real area of your life.
	•	If–Then If I feel harsh, I’ll pair it with context: “Because I want to stay well/keep our relationship healthy…”
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 44
fields.teaching_content:
You can say no and keep the explanation brief.
	•	Prompt Draft: “Thanks for thinking of me; I’m not able to do that.” (Optional: one short reason.)
	•	If–Then If I write a paragraph, I’ll cut it down to one sentence.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 45
fields.teaching_content:
Taking responsibility for your piece of a conflict makes your words safer.
	•	Prompt Draft: “My part in what happened is…” (one behavior).
	•	If–Then If I’m tempted to say “but you…,” I’ll keep this line focused on me.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 46
fields.teaching_content:
“But” often cancels what came before; “and” holds both truths.
	•	Prompt Rewrite: “I appreciate you, but I need something different” → “I appreciate you, and I need something different.” Then apply to your own situation.
	•	If–Then If it sounds strange, I’ll try it once and watch how it feels.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 47
fields.teaching_content:
Where and when you speak affects how it lands.
	•	Prompt Complete: “For the conversation I need to have, the best time/place might be…” and “I’ll avoid…” (e.g., right before bed, public space).
	•	If–Then If I can’t get ideal timing, I’ll at least avoid the worst moments.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 48
fields.teaching_content:
Even if you don’t fully agree, you can end with a stabilizing line.
	•	Prompt Draft: “Thank you for being willing to talk about this. I’m glad we’re trying to work on it, even if it’s not fully solved yet.”
	•	If–Then If that feels too warm, I’ll shorten it but keep the basic acknowledgment.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 49
fields.teaching_content:
A quick mental checklist makes difficult talks smoother.
	•	Prompt List 3 items for your checklist (e.g., name topic, name intention, use I‑statements, ask how it’s landing).
	•	If–Then If I feel overwhelmed, I’ll keep only the top two items.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 50
fields.teaching_content:
You’re building words that can handle truth and respect at the same time.
	•	Prompt Write 3–5 lines: “The kind of person I want to be in difficult conversations is…”
	•	If–Then If I’m not there yet, I’ll describe the direction, not perfection.

Days 51–60 – Expressing Appreciation, Encouragement, and Positive Feedback
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 51
fields.teaching_content:
Specific appreciation is more nourishing than generic praise.
	•	Prompt Choose someone. Complete: “I appreciate that you…” (describe a clear behavior) “because…” (describe impact).
	•	If–Then If I feel shy, I’ll at least write it today and consider saying it later.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 52
fields.teaching_content:
Naming strengths helps people see themselves more clearly.
	•	Prompt Think of someone you value. Complete: “A strength I see in you is…” and “I saw it when you…”
	•	If–Then If I struggle, I’ll imagine what I’d say in a farewell speech.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 53
fields.teaching_content:
Encouragement is honest about difficulty and still offers hope.
	•	Prompt Draft: “This is genuinely hard, and I still believe you can…” (realistic next step, not magic fix).
	•	If–Then If I tend to say “It’s fine” too quickly, I’ll name the challenge first.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 54
fields.teaching_content:
Clear positive feedback supports performance more than “good job.”
	•	Prompt Rewrite “Nice work” for a real situation: “When you _, it really helped because…”
	•	If–Then If it feels like overkill, I’ll remember people rarely get too specific appreciation.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 55
fields.teaching_content:
Verbalizing what you enjoy deepens connection.
	•	Prompt Complete: “One thing I really enjoy about being with you is…” (pick a specific person and trait/behavior).
	•	If–Then If saying it feels vulnerable, I’ll keep it short but still share it.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 56
fields.teaching_content:
Receiving appreciation gracefully is part of healthy verbal expression.
	•	Prompt Draft a simple response to a compliment: “Thank you, that means a lot,” without minimizing.
	•	If–Then If I usually deflect, I’ll practice this line once this week.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 57
fields.teaching_content:
Praising effort encourages learning more than praising only results.
	•	Prompt Choose a person/activity. Complete: “I really appreciate the effort you put into…”
	•	If–Then If I’m focused on results, I’ll still name one effort I genuinely saw.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 58
fields.teaching_content:
Saying small wins out loud can shift the tone of a relationship or team.
	•	Prompt Complete: “One micro‑win from today that I could share with someone is…”
	•	If–Then If today feels like a flop, I’ll look for something tiny but real.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 59
fields.teaching_content:
Speaking kindly to yourself out loud changes your inner script over time.
	•	Prompt Write one sentence of self‑acknowledgment starting with: “I’m proud that I…”
	•	If–Then If that feels cheesy, I’ll phrase it as “I’m glad that I even tried to…”
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 60
fields.teaching_content:
You’re learning to use words not just to fix problems, but to water what’s working.
	•	Prompt Write 3–5 lines: “If I keep expressing appreciation and encouragement more clearly, I think the impact will be…”
	•	If–Then If I’m unsure, I’ll imagine how I would feel receiving what I just wrote.

Days 61–70 – Integrated Verbal Expression for Interpersonal Management
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 61
fields.teaching_content:
Everyone has a default verbal style: fast/slow, blunt/careful, detailed/big‑picture.
	•	Prompt Complete: “If I had to describe my current speaking style in three words, they would be…”
	•	If–Then If I struggle, I’ll ask someone close to offer 1–2 words.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 62
fields.teaching_content:
Certain roles benefit from particular styles—clear and calm for leadership, warm and concise for customer work, etc.
	•	Prompt Write 3–5 lines: “Given my role, the kind of verbal communicator I want to be is…”
	•	If–Then If that feels far away, I’ll describe it as a direction rather than a current reality.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 63
fields.teaching_content:
Your words feel most powerful when they match your values (e.g., honesty, respect, courage).
	•	Prompt Complete: “One value I want my speech to reflect is…” and “That might sound like…” (write a sample sentence).
	•	If–Then If I can’t pick a value, I’ll choose one I admire in others.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 64
fields.teaching_content:
Congruence means your words, tone, and non‑verbals all tell the same story.
	•	Prompt Recall a mismatch. Write: “My words said , but my tone/body said .” Then: “Next time, I want all three to say…”
	•	If–Then If I’m not sure how to align them, I’ll start by adjusting just tone.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 65
fields.teaching_content:
Under stress, we often revert to old verbal habits.
	•	Prompt Complete: “My default under conflict is to…” and “One sentence I want to practice instead is…” (e.g., “I want to understand your view before I respond.”).
	•	If–Then If I forget in the moment, I’ll rehearse it once a day this week.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 66
fields.teaching_content:
Your supportive words can be practical (“What do you need?”), emotional (“That sounds painful”), or both.
	•	Prompt Draft one simple supportive sentence you can actually imagine saying this week.
	•	If–Then If it sounds too formal, I’ll rewrite it in language I’d naturally use.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 67
fields.teaching_content:
The way you communicate decisions shapes how people experience fairness and trust.
	•	Prompt Think of a recent or upcoming decision. Complete: “To communicate this well, I need to explain…” (what, why, impact, support).
	•	If–Then If I’d usually only say “what,” I’ll add at least “why.”
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 68
fields.teaching_content:
A short routine (breath + intention + key sentence) can reset you before high‑stakes conversations.
	•	Prompt Design a 30–60 second reset: e.g., 3 breaths, silently name intention, recall one key sentence. Write it out.
	•	If–Then If I think I won’t remember, I’ll keep it to two simple steps.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 69
fields.teaching_content:
Skill change is easier to keep going when you notice small wins.
	•	Prompt Complete: “One moment recently when I expressed myself more clearly or kindly than I would have in the past was…”
	•	If–Then If I can’t find one, I’ll watch for the next small win this week.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.teaching_content:
You’ve practiced clarity, listening, emotional attunement, and audience flexibility for 70 days.
	•	Prompt Write 3–5 lines starting: “I am becoming someone who can say what’s true and needed, in a way that others can actually hear, by…”
	•	If–Then If I doubt that, I’ll treat these words as a direction, not a verdict.

If you want, I can next turn this into a structured table (Day, Title, Teaching, Prompt, If–Then, Button) so your team can import it into your content system alongside the Empathy journey.

fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 1
fields.teaching_content: : Motivation isn’t always a burst of energy. Sometimes it’s quiet resolve: “I’ll do this even though I don’t feel like it.”
fields.practice_content:
: Think of a time you did something despite not feeling motivated. What kept you going? Write that driver here.
If–Then: If I feel my energy is low, then I will remind myself of my "quiet resolve" driver.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 2
fields.teaching_content: : Some people are morning-motivated; others build steam throughout the day. Knowing your pattern lets you work with it, not against it.
fields.practice_content:
: When in the day do you feel most driven to act? When do you feel least? Map your motivation pattern here.
If–Then: If it is my low-drive time of day, then I will only attempt low-friction tasks.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 3
fields.teaching_content: : Motivation often follows action, not the other way around. Starting—even badly—creates the momentum that fuels motivation.
fields.practice_content:
: Pick a task you’ve been waiting to “feel motivated” for. Start it for just 2 minutes. Did motivation appear? Note what happened.
If–Then: If I am waiting to "feel like it," then I will start the task for exactly 2 minutes.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 4
fields.teaching_content: : Motivation killers include unclear goals, lack of progress, exhaustion, and feeling your effort doesn’t matter. Name yours.
fields.practice_content:
: List your top 3 motivation drains. Which one hits you most often? Write one small thing you could do about it.
If–Then: If a top motivator killer appears, then I will take the one small action I planned.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 5
fields.teaching_content: : Motivation fuels include purpose, progress, autonomy, mastery, and connection. Knowing your fuel lets you seek it deliberately.
fields.practice_content:
: When are you most motivated? What’s present in those moments (purpose, progress, choice, connection)? Name your top fuel.
If–Then: If I need a drive boost, then I will deliberately seek out my "top fuel."
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 6
fields.teaching_content: : External rewards (money, praise) drive short-term effort. Internal rewards (meaning, growth) drive long-term persistence.
fields.practice_content:
: Think of a current goal. Is your motivation mostly internal or external? Write what would make the internal motivation stronger.
If–Then: If I feel I'm only working for praise, then I will identify one way this goal helps me grow.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 7
fields.teaching_content: : When motivation is low, shrink the task to its smallest possible version. “Write one sentence” beats “write the report.”
fields.practice_content:
: Name a task you’re avoiding. What’s the tiniest version you could do in under 2 minutes? Do it now and note what happened.
If–Then: If I am avoiding a large task, then I will perform its tiniest 2-minute version.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 8
fields.teaching_content: : Everyone carries a story about their motivation: “I’m lazy,” “I only work under pressure,” “I lose interest.” Name yours honestly.
fields.practice_content:
: Complete: “The story I tell myself about my motivation is ___.” Is that story always true? Write a more accurate version.
If–Then: If I hear the "lazy" story in my head, then I will recite my accurate motivation story.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 9
fields.teaching_content: : Bad moods suppress motivation. You don’t have to fix your mood first—but acknowledging it helps you adjust expectations.
fields.practice_content:
: Notice your mood right now. How is it affecting your drive to act? Write one task you’ll do despite your current mood.
If–Then: If I am in a bad mood, then I will complete my one "despite the mood" task.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 10
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve explored your motivation patterns, fuels, and drains. Understanding what drives you is the first step to strengthening it.
fields.practice_content:
: Rate your self-awareness about motivation 1–10. What’s the most useful thing you’ve learned? Log it here.
If–Then: If I lose focus, then I will recall the most useful insight from these first 10 days.
Phase 2: Finding Meaning in Tasks
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 11
fields.teaching_content: : A boring task becomes meaningful when linked to a bigger “why.” Filing taxes serves financial freedom. Exercise serves longevity.
fields.practice_content:
: Pick a task you dread. Complete: “This task matters because it leads to ___.” Write the connection here.
If–Then: If a task feels pointless, then I will state exactly how it connects to my bigger "why."
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 12
fields.teaching_content: : Tasks feel more meaningful when you see who benefits—your future self, your family, your team, your community.
fields.practice_content:
: For a current task, answer: “Who benefits when I complete this?” Name the person or group. Does it shift your motivation? Note it.
If–Then: If I feel selfish or isolated in a task, then I will name who else benefits from my success.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 13
fields.teaching_content: : Feeling forced kills motivation. Even small choices—when to start, where to work, how to approach it—restore a sense of control.
fields.practice_content:
: For a task you’re dreading, find one element you can choose (timing, method, location). Make that choice and note the effect.
If–Then: If I feel forced to work, then I will exercise my autonomy over the timing or location.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 14
fields.teaching_content: : Seeing progress—even tiny progress—is one of the strongest motivation boosters. Track it visibly.
fields.practice_content:
: Start tracking progress on one goal today (checkmarks, a tally, a journal line). At day’s end, does seeing progress help? Note it.
If–Then: If I feel like I'm standing still, then I will look at my visible progress tracker.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 15
fields.teaching_content: : Tell yourself: “I’ll work on this for just 10 minutes. After that, I can stop.” Most people keep going. The start is the hardest part.
fields.practice_content:
: Try the 10-minute agreement on a task you’re resisting. Did you stop at 10 or keep going? Write what happened.
If–Then: If resistance is too high, then I will make a 10-minute agreement to start.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 16
fields.teaching_content: : Your brain responds to celebration. A small fist-pump, a mental “yes!”, or checking a box releases dopamine that fuels the next task.
fields.practice_content:
: Complete 3 small tasks today and deliberately celebrate each one (any way you like). Did celebrating change your energy? Note it.
If–Then: If I finish a micro-task, then I will take a moment to celebrate the win.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 17
fields.teaching_content: : When a task feels dull, find one curious question in it: “What if I tried it this way?” Curiosity activates your brain’s reward system.
fields.practice_content:
: Take a boring task and find one genuinely curious question about it. Pursue that question. Did it make the task more engaging?
If–Then: If a task is dull, then I will ask one "what if" question to spark curiosity.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 18
fields.teaching_content: : Tasks that align with your values feel naturally motivating. Tasks that conflict with your values drain energy.
fields.practice_content:
: List 3 current tasks. For each, rate how aligned it is with your values (1–10). What do you notice about the low-scoring ones?
If–Then: If energy is draining, then I will check if the task is aligned with my core values.

fields.title: Day 1
fields.teaching_content: : Every problem is a gap between where you are and where you want to be. Defining the gap clearly is the first step to solving it.
fields.practice_content:
: Name one current problem. Write where you are now and where you want to be. What is the gap? Define it here.

fields.title: Day 2
fields.teaching_content: : A complaint names what’s wrong. A problem definition names what’s wrong AND what “solved” would look like. Move from complaining to defining.

fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 9
fields.teaching_content: : Feeling stuck usually means you’re trying to solve the wrong problem, missing information, or using the wrong approach. Diagnose the stuckness.
fields.practice_content:
: Think of something you’re stuck on. Is it unclear definition, missing info, or wrong approach? Name the type of stuckness. Write it.
If–Then: If I'm unsure why I'm stuck, then I will pick one potential reason—definition, info, or approach—and test it.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 10
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve built the skill of defining problems clearly: identifying gaps, root causes, success criteria, and constraints. Definition is half the solution.
fields.practice_content:
: Rate your problem-definition skill 1–10. What’s one problem you defined more clearly than usual? Log it here.
If–Then: If I rate my skill low, then I will note one specific win from this week to build momentum.
Phase 2: Generating Solutions
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 11
fields.teaching_content: : Generate solutions first, evaluate later. Judging ideas while brainstorming kills creativity. Quantity first, quality second.
fields.practice_content:
: Pick a problem. Set a 5-minute timer and list every possible solution—no filtering. How many ideas did you generate? Write them.
If–Then: If I judge an idea while brainstorming, then I will pause, note the judgment, and add two more wild ideas.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 12
fields.teaching_content: : Often the simplest, most obvious solution works. Before getting creative, ask: “What’s the straightforward fix?” Try it before overcomplicating.
fields.practice_content:
: For a current problem, name the most obvious solution. Would it work? If so, try it. If not, write why not.
If–Then: If the obvious solution doesn't work, then I will resist frustration and look for the next simplest option.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 13
fields.teaching_content: : Instead of “How do I fix this?” try “How could I make this worse?” Reversing often reveals hidden assumptions and new solutions.
fields.practice_content:
: Take a problem and ask: “How could I make this worse?” List 3 ways. Now reverse them into solutions. Write your approach.
If–Then: If I can't imagine making it worse, then I will list the most ridiculous ways I could fail to help spark the reverse.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 14
fields.teaching_content: : Most problems have been solved by someone, somewhere. Look for existing solutions before inventing new ones.
fields.practice_content:
: For a current problem, search for how others have solved something similar. What solution can you borrow or adapt? Write it.
If–Then: If I can't find a similar solution, then I will search for an analogy in a completely unrelated field.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 15
fields.teaching_content: : Introduce a random element (a word, an object, a constraint) and force-connect it to your problem. This breaks fixed thinking patterns.
fields.practice_content:
: Open a book to a random word. Connect that word to your current problem. What new idea does the forced connection produce? Write it.
If–Then: If the random word makes no sense, then I will force a connection by asking, "how does this shape the problem?"
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 16
fields.teaching_content: : Adding a constraint often sparks creativity: “Solve this with zero budget” or “Solve this in one hour.” Limits breed inventiveness.
fields.practice_content:
: Take a problem and add a creative constraint (no money, no technology, only 10 minutes). What solution appears? Write it.
If–Then: If the constraint feels impossible, then I will aim for a "half-baked" version that meets the limit.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 17
fields.teaching_content: : Ask “What if?” questions to explore possibilities: “What if time wasn’t an issue?” “What if I had unlimited help?” Each opens new paths.
fields.practice_content:
: For a current problem, ask 3 “what if” questions. Write the questions and whatever solutions they suggest.
If–Then: If my "what if" questions are too safe, then I will ask one that assumes I have unlimited resources.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 18
fields.teaching_content: : After generating options, evaluate each: what are the pros, cons, and risks? A simple comparison often reveals the best choice.
fields.practice_content:
: Take your top 3 solutions for a problem. Write 2 pros and 2 cons for each. Which one has the best overall balance? Note it.
If–Then: If the pros and cons are tied, then I will choose the one that aligns most with my long-term goal.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 19
fields.teaching_content: : Perfect solutions don’t exist. Choose the “good enough” solution and iterate. Action with an imperfect plan beats inaction with a perfect one.
fields.practice_content:
: For a problem you’ve been overthinking, name the “good enough” solution. What makes it good enough? Commit to trying it. Write it.
If–Then: If I feel tempted to make it perfect, then I will consciously lower my standards to "good enough" to get started.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 20
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve generated solutions through brainstorming, reversal, borrowing, constraints, and “what if” thinking. Your solution toolkit is growing.
fields.practice_content:
: Rate your solution-generation skill 1–10. What’s one technique that produced an idea you wouldn’t have found otherwise? Log it.
If–Then: If I feel I haven't generated good ideas, then I will look at my list and choose one "weird" idea to refine.
Phase 3: Testing and Iterating
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 21
fields.teaching_content: : Don’t invest heavily in a solution before testing it small. A quick, low-cost test tells you more than weeks of planning.
fields.practice_content:
: For a solution you’re considering, design a small, fast test. What would you try, and what result would tell you it works? Write it.
If–Then: If I'm afraid to test, then I will design the smallest, lowest-stakes experiment possible.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 22
fields.teaching_content: : After testing a solution, gather feedback: did it work? Partially? Not at all? Feedback is data that guides the next iteration.
fields.practice_content:
: Test a small solution today. Gather feedback (results, reactions, data). Write what you learned and what you’d adjust.
If–Then: If the feedback is discouraging, then I will treat it as "data" rather than a personal critique.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 23
fields.teaching_content: : When a solution partially works, most people abandon it. Instead, iterate: adjust the parts that didn’t work and keep what did.
fields.practice_content:
: Think of a solution that partially worked. What part succeeded? What part needs adjustment? Write your iteration plan.
If–Then: If I want to abandon a partial solution, then I will list one small element that did work to build on.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 24
fields.teaching_content: : Quick failures teach faster than slow successes. Aim to fail cheaply and early so you can redirect before investing too much.
fields.practice_content:
: For a current problem, what’s the fastest, cheapest way to test your idea and learn? Design a “fail fast” experiment. Write it.
If–Then: If I fear failure, then I will define exactly what "failing safely" looks like before I start.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 25
fields.teaching_content: : Most problems require 3–5 attempts to solve well. The first attempt is rarely the best. Expect iteration, not perfection.
fields.practice_content:
: For a problem you’re working on, are you on attempt 1, 2, or 5? What did each attempt teach you? Write your iteration count.
If–Then: If I get discouraged by attempt #2, then I will remind myself that the best solutions often require more iterations.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 26
fields.teaching_content: : Sometimes fixing one problem creates a new one. Anticipate second-order effects: “If I solve X, what new issue might Y create?”
fields.practice_content:
: For a solution you’re implementing, ask: “What new problems could this create?” Write one potential side effect and a mitigation.
If–Then: If I worry about new problems, then I will list the risk and one simple mitigation for it.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 27
fields.teaching_content: : When your approach clearly isn’t working, pivoting isn’t failure—it’s intelligent adaptation. Know when to keep iterating vs. when to change direction.
fields.practice_content:
: Is there a current approach that needs a pivot, not another tweak? Write the signs telling you it’s time to change direction.
If–Then: If I'm unsure whether to pivot, then I will look for one piece of evidence that the current approach is stalling.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 28
fields.teaching_content: : Without measurement, you can’t tell if your solution is working. Define 1–2 simple metrics: what number or outcome will tell you it’s working?
fields.practice_content:
: For a current problem, define one metric that shows progress. What does improvement look like in numbers or observable outcomes? Write it.
If–Then: If I can't find a metric, then I will look for a simple observation—"did I see X happen?"—as my measure.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 29
fields.teaching_content: : Keeping a brief log of what you tried and what happened prevents repeating failed experiments and shows patterns over time.
fields.practice_content:
: For a current problem, write a log: attempt, approach, result, lesson. Even 1–2 entries build a valuable problem-solving record.
If–Then: If I forget to log my attempts, then I will set a recurring alarm to spend 2 minutes reviewing my day.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 30
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve built a test-and-iterate habit. Problem solving is now a loop: try, observe, adjust, repeat. That loop is the cognitive loop.
fields.practice_content:
: Rate your test-and-iterate skill 1–10. How comfortable are you with imperfect first attempts? Log it.
If–Then: If I struggle to be comfortable with "imperfect", then I will celebrate one "good enough" attempt I made.
Phase 4: Cognitive Flexibility
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 31
fields.teaching_content: : Cognitive flexibility means switching strategies when the current one doesn’t work—without panic. It’s not failure; it’s information.
fields.practice_content:
: Recall a time your first strategy failed. How quickly did you switch? What helped you try a different approach? Write your answer.
If–Then: If I panic when a strategy fails, then I will take 5 minutes to write down what the failure taught me.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 32
fields.teaching_content: : Reframing a problem (“Instead of cutting costs, how do I increase value?”) can unlock solutions invisible from the original angle.
fields.practice_content:
: Take a current problem and reframe it from a completely different angle. Write the original frame and the new one. Do new solutions appear?
If–Then: If I feel stuck on the current angle, then I will physically change my location to force a new perspective.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 33
fields.teaching_content: : Asking someone else for their perspective is not weakness—it’s a problem-solving strategy. Others see what you can’t from inside the problem.
fields.practice_content:
: Share a current problem with someone and ask for their take. Write what they saw that you didn’t. Did their perspective help?
If–Then: If I'm hesitant to ask for help, then I will reframe the request as a "collaborative brainstorming" session.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 34
fields.teaching_content: : Working memory lets you hold multiple parts of a problem in mind while rearranging them. Offload to paper when it gets heavy.
fields.practice_content:
: For a complex problem, write all its pieces on paper or sticky notes. Rearrange them physically. Did externalizing help you think? Note it.
If–Then: If my brain feels crowded, then I will stop thinking and start writing every piece on separate notes.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 35
fields.teaching_content: : Ask: “What other problem is this like?” If it’s like a traffic jam, the solution might involve better flow, not more roads.
fields.practice_content:
: Take a current problem and find an analogy from another field. What solution does the analogy suggest? Write the analogy and idea.
If–Then: If I can't think of an analogy, then I will look at nature for a pattern that matches my problem.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 36
fields.teaching_content: : Mental set is the tendency to use the same approach repeatedly. Deliberately try the opposite of your usual approach.
fields.practice_content:
: For a recurring problem, name your usual approach. Now try the opposite. What happens? Write what you tried and the result.
If–Then: If I find myself repeating the same approach, then I will force myself to do the absolute opposite.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 37
fields.teaching_content: : Your unconscious mind continues processing problems during sleep and idle time. After deep thinking, step away and let your brain work.
fields.practice_content:
: Before bed, briefly review a problem you’re stuck on. Don’t try to solve it—just hold it in mind. In the morning, write any new ideas.
If–Then: If I wake up without a solution, then I will trust that my subconscious is still processing and stay curious.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 38
fields.teaching_content: : Two partial solutions can combine into one full solution. Look for complementary ideas that cover each other’s weaknesses.
fields.practice_content:
: Take two partial solutions you’ve tried for the same problem. Could they combine? Write the hybrid solution.
If–Then: If the hybrid solution feels messy, then I will focus on the single most promising part and refine that.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 39
fields.teaching_content: : Sometimes solutions arrive suddenly—the “aha” moment. Insight comes after sustained effort followed by mental rest. Trust the process.
fields.practice_content:
: Recall an “aha” moment in your life. What had you been doing before the insight hit? Was there effort, then rest? Write the sequence.
If–Then: If no insight comes, then I will step away from the problem entirely to let my brain rest.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 40
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve built cognitive flexibility: reframing, strategy-switching, analogies, and combining ideas. Your problem-solving loop is getting faster.
fields.practice_content:
: Rate your cognitive flexibility 1–10. How easily can you switch strategies when one fails? Log it.
If–Then: If I find it hard to switch strategies, then I will practice "giving up" on a minor tactic to build the muscle.
Phase 5: Complex Problem Solving
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 41
fields.teaching_content: : Some problems have no single right answer—only trade-offs. The skill is choosing the best trade-off given your constraints and values.
fields.practice_content:
: Name a problem with no clear answer. What are the top 2 trade-offs? Which aligns better with your values? Write your choice and why.
If–Then: If I'm paralyzed by trade-offs, then I will pick the one that feels 5% more aligned with my values.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 42
fields.teaching_content: : You’ll rarely have all the information you need. Make the best decision you can with 70% of the data, then adjust as you learn more.
fields.practice_content:
: Face a problem where you’re missing information. Decide anyway with what you have. Note what you’d do differently with more data.
If–Then: If I fear making a decision with incomplete info, then I will set a "check-in" date to re-evaluate.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 43
fields.teaching_content: : Complex problems have chains: solving A enables B, which enables C. Map the chain to find the first domino to push.
fields.practice_content:
: Take a complex problem and map its chain of sub-problems. Which sub-problem, once solved, unlocks the most progress? Write the chain.
If–Then: If I'm overwhelmed by the chain of problems, then I will ignore everything except the very first step.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 44
fields.teaching_content: : Two brains beat one. Collaborative problem solving leverages different perspectives, knowledge, and creative styles.
fields.practice_content:
: Work on a problem with someone else today. What did they contribute that you wouldn’t have alone? Write the collaborative outcome.
If–Then: If I feel I must do it alone, then I will invite one person to just listen while I talk through the process.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 45
fields.teaching_content: : Fear of failure, attachment to one approach, or ego can block solutions. Emotions are part of the loop—notice them without letting them steer.
fields.practice_content:
: Is an emotion blocking your problem solving right now (fear, pride, frustration)? Name it and set it aside. What opens up? Write it.
If–Then: If I feel ego getting in the way, then I will ask, "what would I advise a friend to do?"
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 46
fields.teaching_content: : The best solutions often emerge from the tightest constraints. Unlimited resources can actually make problem solving harder.
fields.practice_content:
: Name a constraint on a current problem. Instead of resenting it, use it as a creative guide. What solution does it suggest? Write it.
If–Then: If a constraint feels like a burden, then I will write down three ways it actually protects me.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 47
fields.teaching_content: : What’s the smallest solution that addresses the core problem? Start there. You can always expand later, but starting small builds momentum.
fields.practice_content:
: For a current problem, define the minimum viable solution: what’s the simplest thing that would improve the situation? Write it.
If–Then: If I find myself adding features, then I will strip it back to the absolute bare minimum needed to start.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 48
fields.teaching_content:
Problem Solving
Teaching: Explaining your problem-solving process to someone else reveals your approach and strengthens your methodology.
fields.practice_content:
: Walk someone through how you’d solve a problem step by step. What 3 principles guide your approach? Write them.
If–Then: If I can't explain my process, then I will write down my steps as if teaching a beginner.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 49
fields.teaching_content: : Keeping a log of problems, approaches, and outcomes over time builds a personal problem-solving playbook.
fields.practice_content:
: Start a problem journal: write today’s problem, your approach, and the result. Even one entry starts the habit. Log it here.
If–Then: If I don't feel like journaling, then I will write just one sentence about what I tried today.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 50
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve tackled ambiguity, incomplete info, collaboration, and emotional blocks. Your problem-solving loop is robust and adaptive.
fields.practice_content:
: Rate your complex problem-solving ability 1–10. What’s the biggest shift in how you approach problems? Log it.
If–Then: If I feel my progress has stalled, then I will look at my logs to see how far I've come.
Phase 6: Integration and Identity
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 51
fields.teaching_content: : You now have tools: gap definition, brainstorming, testing, iterating, reframing, analogy, collaboration, minimum viable solutions. Top 3?
fields.practice_content:
: List the 3 problem-solving tools you rely on most. When does each one help? Write your toolkit here.
If–Then: If I forget my tools, then I will keep my top 3 written on a sticky note where I can see them.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 52
fields.teaching_content: : Each problem you solve builds evidence that you can handle what life throws at you. Problem solving is applied confidence.
fields.practice_content:
: Complete: “Because I can solve problems, I trust myself to handle ___.” Write your answer here.
If–Then: If I doubt my ability, then I will recall one problem I successfully solved in the past.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 53
fields.teaching_content: : Everyone has one: jumping to solutions too fast, avoiding the hard part, quitting too early, or working alone when help is needed.
fields.practice_content:
: What’s your #1 problem-solving weak spot? Write one specific strategy to compensate. Log it here.
If–Then: If I find myself using my "weak spot" approach, then I will pause and intentionally use one of my "strength" tools instead.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 54
fields.teaching_content: : The problems you choose to solve reflect your values and purpose. Choosing meaningful problems makes the effort worthwhile.
fields.practice_content:
: What kind of problems are you most drawn to solving? How does this connect to your values or purpose? Write your answer.
If–Then: If I feel disconnected from the problem, then I will ask how solving it serves my larger goals.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 55
fields.teaching_content:
the Loop
Teaching: Explaining the cognitive loop (define gap → generate solutions → test → iterate) to someone else solidifies your own mastery.
fields.practice_content:
: Explain the problem-solving loop to an imagined friend in 3 sentences. What 3 tips would you add? Write your explanation.
If–Then: If I struggle to explain the loop, then I will draw it out as a simple diagram.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 56
fields.teaching_content: : Apply the full cognitive loop to a life-level problem: define the gap, brainstorm, test small, iterate. Big problems use the same loop.
fields.practice_content:
: Name a life-level problem. Write the gap, 3 possible solutions, and one small test you can run this week. Log your plan.
If–Then: If a life-level problem feels too big, then I will treat it as a series of small, solvable daily tasks.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 57
fields.teaching_content: : Recurring problems signal that the root cause hasn’t been addressed. Dig deeper: solve the system, not just the symptom.
fields.practice_content:
: Name a problem that keeps coming back. What root cause might be driving it? Write the symptom and the deeper issue.
If–Then: If I keep hitting the same root cause, then I will change my environment to make the old way impossible.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 58
fields.teaching_content: : Know your warning signs: avoiding the problem, overthinking without acting, repeating failed approaches, or quitting too early.
fields.practice_content:
: List 3 red flags that tell you your problem solving is off track. What’s your correction for each? Write them.
If–Then: If I see a red flag, then I will immediately stop and execute my planned correction.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 59
fields.teaching_content: : Sustainable problem solving: define daily, brainstorm weekly, test monthly, review quarterly. Build the loop into your rhythm.
fields.practice_content:
: Design your problem-solving routine. When do you define, brainstorm, test, and review? Write your plan here.
If–Then: If I skip my routine, then I will forgive myself and just focus on the next step in the loop.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 60
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve spent 60 days training the cognitive loop. You define gaps, generate options, test, and iterate. You’re a problem solver by practice.
fields.practice_content:
: Complete: “I am someone who solves problems by ___. When I’m stuck, I ___.” Save this as your problem-solving identity statement.
If–Then: If I feel unsure, then I will trust the 60 days of practice as my foundation and take the next step.

Badge 2 (Day 20): “The Solution Generator”
Unlock message: You’ve moved from complaining to creating, filling your toolkit with endless possibilities.
Popup: You’re generating ideas faster than the obstacles can keep up.

Badge 3 (Day 30): “The Iterative Tester”
Unlock message: You treat every attempt as valuable data, not a final judgment.
Popup: You’re failing fast and refining your path with every experiment.

Badge 4 (Day 40): “The Cognitive Flexer”
Unlock message: You can pivot your perspective and switch strategies the moment the old one stalls.
Popup: You’re thinking with fluidity, mastering the switch.

Badge 5 (Day 50): “The Complexity Navigator”
Unlock message: You’ve learned to hold messy, ambiguous pieces together until the solution emerges.
Popup: You’re navigating the unknown with calm confidence.

Badge 6 (Day 60): “The Integrated Problem Solver”
Unlock message: Problem-solving is no longer a task—it is part of who you are and how you live.

fields.title: Day 1
fields.teaching_content: : Most people jump into tasks without a roadmap. Today, just notice: do you plan before acting, or figure it out as you go? Awareness is step one.
fields.practice_content:
: Think of one task you did today. Did you plan it or wing it? Type what you notice about your default style.
If–Then: If I notice myself winging a task, then I will pause and name the first step.
