fields.title: Day 2
fields.teaching_content: : Planning means naming what needs to happen before you start. Even a rough list of steps beats no list at all. Start small.
fields.practice_content:
: Pick a task for tomorrow. Write 3–5 steps you’d need to complete it, in any order. Just list them here.
If–Then: If I feel blank, then I will write down three basic steps to complete the task.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 3
fields.teaching_content: : Before starting a task, mentally walk through it like a movie. This “mental rehearsal” activates the same brain regions as doing it.
fields.practice_content:
: Choose a task for today. Close your eyes and mentally walk through each step. Note one thing you noticed that you’d have missed.
If–Then: If I start a task too fast, then I will take 30 seconds to visualize the steps.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 4
fields.teaching_content: : Skipping planning often has hidden costs: wasted time, forgotten steps, extra stress. Seeing those costs builds motivation to plan.
fields.practice_content:
: Recall a time you jumped in without a plan and hit a snag. What step, if planned, would have prevented it? Write it here.
If–Then: If I hit a barrier, then I will note one specific step that would have avoided it.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 5
fields.teaching_content: : Your memory already holds planning wins. Recalling them builds trust that the effort of planning pays off.
fields.practice_content:
: Think of a time planning ahead made something go smoothly. What did you plan that made the difference? Note it here.
If–Then: If I am rushing, then I will remind myself of a past time when planning saved me stress.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 6
fields.teaching_content: : A plan doesn’t need to be long. Even two minutes of thinking “what do I need and in what order?” dramatically reduces chaos.
fields.practice_content:
: Before your next task today, set a 2-minute timer and jot a quick plan. After, note whether those 2 minutes helped.
If–Then: If I feel overwhelmed, then I will set a 2-minute timer for a quick plan.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 7
fields.teaching_content: : Planning has an endpoint: you start. Overthinking loops without action. A good plan is “good enough,” not perfect.
fields.practice_content:
: Think of something you’ve been overthinking. Write 3 concrete next steps and a time you’ll start. That’s your plan.
If–Then: If I find myself overthinking, then I will set a hard stop and write down 3 action steps.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 8
fields.teaching_content: : Common blockers: “It takes too long,” “I work better spontaneously,” or “I don’t know where to start.” Name yours.
fields.practice_content:
: Complete: “I tend to skip planning because ___.” Then ask: is that always true, or just a habit? Type your answer.
If–Then: If I use an excuse to skip planning, then I will ask myself if it's a habit or a reality.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 9
fields.teaching_content: : Small tasks (making coffee) need little planning. Bigger tasks need more. Today, notice which of your tasks actually deserve a plan.
fields.practice_content:
: List 3 tasks from today. Rate each: “no plan needed,” “quick plan,” or “real plan needed.” Type your ratings.
If–Then: If I am unsure of the plan's size, then I will aim for a 'quick plan' rather than no plan.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 10
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve spent 10 days noticing your planning habits. You don’t need to be a planner yet—just more aware of when planning helps.
fields.practice_content:
: On a 1–10 scale, how aware are you now of when you need a plan? What’s one thing you’ve noticed? Log it here.
If–Then: If I lose focus on awareness, then I will note one small task today that benefited from a plan.
Phase 2: Breaking Tasks Into Steps
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 11
fields.teaching_content: : Big tasks feel overwhelming because your brain tries to hold everything at once. Breaking them into pieces frees up mental space.
fields.practice_content:
: Pick one task that feels big. Break it into at least 4 smaller pieces. Write them here—don’t worry about order yet.
If–Then: If a task feels like a mountain, then I will break it into 4 tiny hills.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 12
fields.teaching_content: : Before starting, ask: “What materials, info, or people do I need?” Missing resources mid-task is the #1 plan-killer.
fields.practice_content:
: Choose a task for tomorrow. List everything you’ll need to complete it (tools, info, help). Note anything you need to gather first.
If–Then: If I get stuck mid-task, then I will stop and list the materials or info I’m missing.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 13
fields.teaching_content: : When you can’t see the whole path, just define the very first step. One clear first step beats a foggy full plan.
fields.practice_content:
: Think of something you’ve been putting off. What is the single first physical action? (e.g., “open laptop,” “text Sam”). Type it.
If–Then: If I feel paralyzed by the whole project, then I will focus only on the first physical action.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 14
fields.teaching_content: : Vague steps stall you. “Work on project” is fuzzy. “Draft intro paragraph” is clear. Good steps start with a verb.
fields.practice_content:
: Rewrite 3 tasks on your to-do list so each starts with a specific verb (draft, call, send, measure, list). Type them here.
If–Then: If I write vague steps, then I will rewrite them to start with a specific verb.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 15
fields.teaching_content: : If a step takes more than 20 minutes or feels vague, it’s probably still too big. Break it down further until it feels doable.
fields.practice_content:
: Take one step from yesterday’s list. Can you break it into 2–3 sub-steps? If so, write them. If not, it’s the right size.
If–Then: If a step feels too big, then I will break it into 2 sub-steps immediately.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 16
fields.teaching_content: : Each step needs a clear finish line. Ask: “How will I know this step is done?” If you can’t answer, the step is too vague.
fields.practice_content:
: Pick 3 steps from a current task. For each, write what “done” looks like in one sentence. Type them here.
If–Then: If I am unclear on progress, then I will write one sentence defining what 'done' means.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 17
fields.teaching_content: : Batching similar steps (all emails, all calls, all research) saves mental switching costs and speeds up execution.
fields.practice_content:
: Look at a current task’s steps. Can any be grouped by type? Reorganize them into clusters and note if it feels more efficient.
If–Then: If I am multitasking, then I will group similar steps to finish faster.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 18
fields.teaching_content: : Plans often fail because of invisible steps—things so obvious you forget to list them. Travel time, drying time, waiting for replies.
fields.practice_content:
: Review a plan you’ve made. What hidden or “obvious” step did you leave out? Add it now and type it here.
If–Then: If a plan feels incomplete, then I will pause to identify any 'invisible' steps like travel or waiting.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 19
fields.teaching_content: : Explaining a plan to someone else reveals gaps. If they can’t follow your steps, the plan isn’t clear enough yet.
fields.practice_content:
: Take a current plan and imagine explaining it to a friend. Where would they ask “but how?” That’s your gap. Note it.
If–Then: If I struggle to explain my plan, then I will simplify the steps until they are clear.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 20
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve been practicing breaking tasks into clear, actionable steps. This is the core engine of planning. How does it feel now?
fields.practice_content:
: Complete: “Breaking tasks into steps now feels ___ compared to 10 days ago.” Rate your comfort 1–10 and log it here.
If–Then: If I doubt my breaking-down skills, then I will remind myself that smaller pieces equal more mental space.
Phase 3: Sequencing and Time Estimation
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 21
fields.teaching_content: : Sequencing means asking “what must happen before what?” Some steps depend on others. Finding that order is real planning power.
fields.practice_content:
: List 5 steps for a task. Draw arrows: which step must come before another? Reorder them and type your sequence.
If–Then: If I am stuck on order, then I will draw arrows between steps to find the dependencies.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 22
fields.teaching_content: : Not all steps need to happen in order. Some can run in parallel (e.g., laundry while cooking). Spotting these saves time.
fields.practice_content:
: Look at a current plan. Are any steps independent enough to happen at the same time? Mark them and note the time saved.
If–Then: If I have idle time, then I will scan my plan for steps I can do in parallel.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 23
fields.teaching_content: : Humans consistently underestimate how long tasks take—this is called the “planning fallacy.” Expect things to take 1.5x longer.
fields.practice_content:
: Pick a task for today. Estimate how long it will take, then multiply by 1.5. After you do it, log the actual time here.
If–Then: If I underestimate time, then I will take my initial estimate and multiply it by 1.5.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 24
fields.teaching_content: : Anchor your steps to real time slots (“after lunch,” “9 AM”) instead of leaving them floating. Anchored plans get done more.
fields.practice_content:
: Take 3 steps from a plan and assign each a specific time or time anchor for tomorrow. Write them here.
If–Then: If I feel unanchored, then I will assign a specific time or 'time anchor' to my next 3 steps.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 25
fields.teaching_content: : Plans without buffers crack at the first delay. Adding 10–15 minutes between steps absorbs surprises without derailing you.
fields.practice_content:
: Look at tomorrow’s schedule. Where could you add a 15-minute buffer? Add one and note where you placed it.
If–Then: If my schedule looks fragile, then I will add a 15-minute buffer between major steps.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 26
fields.teaching_content: : If step 2 runs long, what happens to step 3? Knowing your “if late” response keeps one delay from becoming a cascade.
fields.practice_content:
: For a plan this week, pick the step most likely to run over. What will you cut or shift if it does? Write your backup.
If–Then: If I fear being late, then I will decide which step I can cut if I run over.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 27
fields.teaching_content: : Setting when you’ll stop—not just when you’ll start—prevents tasks from expanding to fill all your time.
fields.practice_content:
: For your next work block, set both a start and end time. Afterward, note: did the end time help you focus? Log it.
If–Then: If I am drifting in time, then I will set a clear end-time for this task.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 28
fields.teaching_content: : Plan hard thinking for your high-energy hours and routine steps for low-energy times. Sequence by energy, not just logic.
fields.practice_content:
: When is your peak energy today? Place your hardest planning step there. Note your energy pattern here.
If–Then: If my energy dips, then I will shift a routine step to this time slot.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 29
fields.teaching_content: : Long plans need checkpoints. A milestone is a mini-finish-line that tells you you’re on track and gives a sense of progress.
fields.practice_content:
: Take a multi-day plan and insert 2 milestones. What will you have completed at each? Write them here.
If–Then: If the goal feels too far, then I will mark a mini-finish-line to track progress.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 30
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve been learning to sequence steps, estimate time, and build realistic timelines. These skills turn lists into real plans.
fields.practice_content:
: Rate your ability to sequence and time-estimate on a 1–10 scale. What’s one thing you do differently now? Log it.
If–Then: If I feel inefficient, then I will try one new sequencing technique today.
Phase 4: Anticipating Obstacles
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 31
fields.teaching_content: : Good planners don’t ignore risk—they name it. Asking “what could go wrong?” isn’t pessimism, it’s preparation.
fields.practice_content:
: Pick an upcoming plan. List 2 things that could realistically go wrong. Just name them—no solution needed yet.
If–Then: If I feel optimistic about the plan, then I will force myself to name 2 things that could go wrong.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 32
fields.teaching_content: : For each risk, a simple “if X, then I’ll Y” backup keeps you moving instead of freezing when things go sideways.
fields.practice_content: : Take yesterday’s 2 risks. Write an “
fields.real_life_plan:
” backup for each. (e.g., “If the file isn’t ready, then I’ll work on section 2.”)
If–Then: If a risk seems likely, then I will write an 'If-Then' backup for it now.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 33
fields.teaching_content: : A bottleneck is the one step that everything else waits on. Identifying it lets you protect or fast-track it.
fields.practice_content:
: In a current plan, which single step would delay everything if it stalled? That’s your bottleneck. Name it here.
If–Then: If I am worried about the deadline, then I will identify the bottleneck step and protect it.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 34
fields.teaching_content: : Plans that rely on others need extra lead time. People have their own timelines. Build in waiting-for-others buffers.
fields.practice_content:
: In a current plan, which steps depend on someone else? How much lead time will you give them? Write your answer.
If–Then: If I am waiting on others, then I will add a buffer to that specific step.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 35
fields.teaching_content: : Perfectionism kills plans. At each step, ask: “Is this good enough to move forward?” Progress beats polish.
fields.practice_content:
: Where in a current plan are you likely to over-polish? Set a “good enough” rule for that step and type it here.
If–Then: If I want to make it perfect, then I will stop and ask 'Is this good enough to move forward?'
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 36
fields.teaching_content: : You won’t always feel like executing your plan. Pre-decide what you’ll do on a low-motivation day: smaller version, not zero.
fields.practice_content:
: Write a “low energy version” of one step in your current plan—the minimum you’d still do on a bad day. Log it.
If–Then: If I feel low motivation, then I will execute the 'minimum version' of my plan.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 37
fields.teaching_content: : If a plan isn’t working, changing it isn’t failure—it’s smart. Don’t keep following a bad plan just because you started it.
fields.practice_content:
: Think of a plan you stuck with too long. What signal told you it wasn’t working? What would you do differently? Note it.
If–Then: If a plan is failing, then I will give myself permission to change it rather than forcing it.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 38
fields.teaching_content: : When disrupted, take 60 seconds to re-plan rather than scrambling. A tiny re-plan beats no plan after a curveball.
fields.practice_content:
: Next time something disrupts your plan today, pause for 60 seconds and re-sequence. Note what you adjusted here.
If–Then: If I hit a disruption, then I will take 60 seconds to re-plan instead of panic.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 39
fields.teaching_content: : Every failed plan teaches you something—a missing step, a bad estimate, an ignored risk. Mine those lessons.
fields.practice_content:
: Recall a plan that fell apart. What one lesson does it teach you about how you plan? Write it here.
If–Then: If I fail, then I will note one missing step or bad estimate to learn from.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 40
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve been building obstacle awareness and flexibility. Good planners aren’t rigid—they’re prepared and adaptive.
fields.practice_content:
: Rate your comfort anticipating obstacles 1–10. What’s your go-to strategy when plans go sideways? Log it.
If–Then: If I feel rigid, then I will try to adapt one part of my plan today.
Phase 5: Planning in Complex Situations
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 41
fields.teaching_content: : Stress narrows your thinking and makes plans messier. When stressed, simplify: fewer steps, more buffer, lower ambition.
fields.practice_content:
: Think of a stressful week. How did your planning change? Write one rule for yourself about planning when stressed.
If–Then: If I am stressed, then I will immediately simplify the plan to fewer steps.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 42
fields.teaching_content: : Strong emotions (excitement, anxiety) distort plans. Excitement over-commits; anxiety over-prepares. Notice which you do.
fields.practice_content:
: Recall a plan made while emotional. Was it too ambitious or too cautious? What would a calm version look like? Note it.
If–Then: If I am emotional, then I will pause to see if I am over-committing or over-preparing.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 43
fields.teaching_content: : When your plan involves other people, their needs and timelines matter. Collaborative plans need shared clarity.
fields.practice_content:
: Think of a plan that involves someone else. Have you shared the steps and timeline with them? If not, do it today and note it.
If–Then: If my plan affects others, then I will share the steps with them today.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 44
fields.teaching_content: : Multi-day plans need daily check-ins. Each evening, review tomorrow’s steps and adjust based on today’s progress.
fields.practice_content:
: Tonight, spend 3 minutes reviewing tomorrow’s plan. Adjust one thing based on how today went. Note your adjustment.
If–Then: If I am on a multi-day project, then I will spend 3 minutes tonight reviewing tomorrow’s steps.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 45
fields.teaching_content: : A 15-minute weekly plan (Sunday or Monday) prevents daily firefighting. Zoom out before you zoom in.
fields.practice_content:
: Spend 15 minutes planning your week: list top 3 goals and key steps for each. Note how this overview feels.
If–Then: If I feel like I am firefighting, then I will set aside 15 minutes for a weekly plan.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 46
fields.teaching_content: : Creative work resists rigid plans. Instead, plan the conditions: time, space, and a starting prompt—then let it flow.
fields.practice_content:
: For a creative or open-ended task, plan the conditions (when, where, first prompt) instead of every step. Write your setup.
If–Then: If I have a creative task, then I will plan the 'conditions' rather than the steps.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 47
fields.teaching_content: : Not everything needs a plan. Routine tasks, spontaneous moments, and rest don’t. Over-planning is its own trap.
fields.practice_content:
: Name one area where you over-plan or plan unnecessarily. What would happen if you let it be unplanned? Write your thought.
If–Then: If I am over-planning, then I will pick one area to leave 'unplanned.'
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 48
fields.teaching_content: : A plan in your head helps you. A plan shared with others helps everyone. Say it out loud or write it down for accountability.
fields.practice_content:
: Share one plan with someone today (text, voice, or in person). Note their reaction—did they add anything useful?
If–Then: If I lack accountability, then I will share my plan with someone else.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 49
fields.teaching_content: : After completing a plan, spend 2 minutes asking: what worked, what didn’t, what will I do differently next time?
fields.practice_content:
: Review a recently completed plan. Write one “keep doing” and one “change next time.” Log them here.
If–Then: If I finish a task, then I will spend 2 minutes reviewing what went right or wrong.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 50
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve stretched planning into complex, emotional, and social territory. Planning is becoming a flexible skill, not a rigid formula.
fields.practice_content:
: Rate your overall planning skill 1–10. What’s changed most about how you approach tasks since Day 1? Log it.
If–Then: If I feel stagnant, then I will review how my planning style has evolved since Day 1.
Phase 6: Integration and Identity
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 51
fields.teaching_content: : By now you have many tools: step-breaking, sequencing, time-estimating, buffering, contingencies. Name your top 3.
fields.practice_content:
: List the 3 planning tools you use most. For each, write when you tend to reach for it. Log your toolkit here.
If–Then: If I am unsure which tool to use, then I will revisit my top 3 favorite planning tools.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 52
fields.teaching_content: : Each time you make and follow a plan, you build trust in your own ability to handle what’s ahead. That’s powerful.
fields.practice_content:
: Complete: “Because I can plan, I now trust myself to handle ___.” Write your answer here.
If–Then: If I lose self-trust, then I will focus on completing just one small, planned action.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 53
fields.teaching_content: : Everyone has one: underestimating time, skipping contingencies, over-detailing. Knowing yours helps you compensate.
fields.practice_content:
: What’s your #1 planning weak spot? Write one simple rule to guard against it. (e.g., “Always add 30% more time.”)
If–Then: If I hit my weak spot, then I will apply my pre-set rule to guard against it.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 54
fields.teaching_content: : Plans serve goals, and goals serve values. When a plan feels meaningless, reconnect it to why it matters to you.
fields.practice_content:
: Pick a current plan. Complete: “This plan matters because it serves my value of ___.” Type your answer.
If–Then: If a plan feels meaningless, then I will reconnect it to the value it serves.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 55
fields.teaching_content:
Someone to Plan
Teaching: Explaining planning to someone else deepens your own skill. You notice what you know intuitively and what you can name clearly.
fields.practice_content:
: Imagine teaching a friend to plan a task. What 3 tips would you give? Write them here.
If–Then: If I want to solidify my skills, then I will explain my planning process to a friend.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 56
fields.teaching_content: : Big goals need layered plans: an overall roadmap, monthly milestones, weekly actions, and daily steps. Start from the top.
fields.practice_content:
: Name one big goal. Write the roadmap: 3 milestones and one next-week action step for the first milestone. Log it.
If–Then: If I face a big goal, then I will break it down into milestones and weekly actions.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 57
fields.teaching_content: : Rigid plans break; flexible plans bend. Your skill isn’t making the perfect plan—it’s adjusting when reality shifts.
fields.practice_content:
: Recall a recent plan you had to change. What did you adjust and how quickly? Note what made adapting easier.
If–Then: If the situation changes, then I will adapt the plan rather than complain.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 58
fields.teaching_content: : Know your warning signs: procrastinating the plan itself, vague steps, no time estimates, skipping contingencies.
fields.practice_content:
: List 3 red flags that tell you your planning is slipping. What will you do when you spot one? Write your answer.
If–Then: If I see a red flag, then I will pause to re-evaluate my current approach.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 59
fields.teaching_content: : A sustainable planning habit needs a routine: same time, same trigger, same quick format. Design yours now.
fields.practice_content:
: Design your planning routine: When will you plan? What’s your trigger? What format? (e.g., “Sunday 8 PM, notebook, 15 min.”)
If–Then: If my routine slips, then I will reset my planning trigger and time.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 60
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve spent 60 days building this skill. You’re not someone who “should” plan—you’re someone who does plan, your way.
fields.practice_content:
: Complete: “I am someone who plans by ___. When things go sideways, I ___.” Save this as your planning identity statement.
If–Then: If I doubt my identity, then I will say 'I am a planner who adapts.'
Phase 7: Advanced Planning Mastery
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 61
fields.teaching_content: : Look back at the last 60 days. Which phase was the hardest? Recognizing where you struggled is the first step to mastering it.
fields.practice_content:
: Name the phase that was most difficult. Why? Write one realization about your growth.
If–Then: If I struggle with a phase, then I will recognize it as a growth opportunity.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 62
fields.teaching_content: : Planning isn't just for today; it's for the future. Practice connecting your daily tasks to a 90-day goal.
fields.practice_content:
: Set a goal for 3 months from now. What is one action you can take this week to start?
If–Then: If I lose track of the big picture, then I will set a 90-day goal and one action step.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 63
fields.teaching_content: : The best way to deepen your planning skill is to teach it. Explain your process to someone else.
fields.practice_content:
: Teach one planning tool to a friend or colleague. How did explaining it clarify it for you?
If–Then: If I feel I have mastered a skill, then I will mentor someone else in it.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 64
fields.teaching_content: : High achievers often forget to plan downtime. Plan your rest with the same precision you plan your work.
fields.practice_content:
: Schedule 2 hours of "unplanned" time this weekend. Protect this time in your schedule.
If–Then: If I forget to rest, then I will schedule 2 hours of 'unplanned' time this weekend.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 65
fields.teaching_content: : After 65 days, you have a unique style. What is your strongest planning habit?
fields.practice_content:
: Identify your single greatest planning strength. How can you apply it to a new project?
If–Then: If I feel unsure of my strength, then I will apply my biggest planning habit to a new project.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 66
fields.teaching_content: : The world is unpredictable. Practice "what-if" planning for a project you are currently working on.
fields.practice_content:
: List 3 "what-if" scenarios for your biggest project. Write one mitigation step for each.
If–Then: If I feel vulnerable to the world, then I will practice 'what-if' planning for my current project.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 67
fields.teaching_content: : Habits are automatic. Design a planning ritual that happens at the same time and place every week.
fields.practice_content:
: Define your weekly ritual: Day, Time, Location, and Duration. Write it here.
If–Then: If my habits are slipping, then I will reset my weekly planning ritual.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 68
fields.teaching_content: : Big goals can be intimidating. Practice breaking a massive, multi-year goal into a 1-year roadmap.
fields.practice_content:
: Pick a big goal. What are 4 major milestones for the next year?
If–Then: If the goal is massive, then I will map out the 4 major milestones for the next year.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 69
fields.teaching_content: : Planning is an ongoing loop: Plan, Act, Review, Adjust. Which part of this loop do you need to emphasize more?
fields.practice_content:
: Look at your loop. Are you spending enough time on Review and Adjust? Name one tweak.
If–Then: If I feel the loop is broken, then I will focus entirely on the 'Review' stage.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 70
fields.teaching_content: : You have completed the 70-day program. This is just the beginning of your planning mastery.
fields.practice_content:
: Define your "Planning Identity" statement. How do you plan now, and how will you continue to improve?
If–Then: If I reach the end, then I will define my 'Planning Identity' statement for the future.

3. Label: The Time Navigator Unlock message: You’ve mastered the art of ordering tasks for efficiency. Popup: You’re sequencing your day with rhythm instead of chaos.
4. Label: The Risk Strategist Unlock message: You see hurdles before they become roadblocks. Popup: You’re prepared for the twists in the road ahead.
5. Label: The Adaptive Planner Unlock message: You can pivot your plan when stress or emotions arise. Popup: Your plans are now flexible enough to handle any situation.
6. Label: The Self-Trust Builder Unlock message: Planning is now a reliable part of your self-trust routine. Popup: You trust yourself because you know you can plan your way forward.
7. Label: The Master Strategist Unlock message: You see the big picture and the daily steps with clarity. Popup: You are officially a master of your own roadmap.
Descriptive Badge Set

Badge 4 (Day 40): "The Courageous Observer" – Awarded for learning to stand in the fire of fear and take action despite it.
Badge 5 (Day 50): "The Adaptive Planner" – Awarded for learning to plan effectively even in complex or stressful environments.

fields.title: Day 1
fields.teaching_content: : Being busy is not the same as being productive. Today, notice the difference between tasks that matter and tasks that just fill time.
fields.practice_content:
: List 5 things you did today. Mark each as “mattered” or “just filled time.” What do you notice? Type your answer.
If–Then: If I notice I am filling my time with low-value tasks, then I will identify one high-impact task for tomorrow.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 2
fields.teaching_content: : Most people prioritize by urgency, habit, or whoever asks loudest. Today, just notice: how do you actually decide what to do first?
fields.practice_content:
: Think about how you chose your first task today. Was it urgent, easy, habitual, or truly important? Name your pattern here.
If–Then: If I realize I chose a task because it was "loudest" rather than "important," then I will pause and re-evaluate my priority list.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 3
fields.teaching_content: : Before any task, ask: “If I could only do one thing today, would this be it?” That question reveals real importance fast.
fields.practice_content:
: Look at tomorrow’s to-do list. Ask the “one thing” question for each item. Which one wins? Write it here.
If–Then: If I struggle to identify "the one thing," then I will ask myself which task moves me closest to my long-term goal.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 4
fields.teaching_content: : Urgent tasks scream for attention. Important tasks build your future. They’re often not the same. Learning to tell them apart is key.
fields.practice_content:
: List 3 tasks. Label each: urgent, important, both, or neither. Notice which category you spend the most time in.
If–Then: If I find myself spending all my time on "urgent" tasks, then I will block out time for one "important" task before the end of the day.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 5
fields.teaching_content: : Every yes is a no to something else. Today, notice what you give up each time you agree to a task or request.
fields.practice_content:
: Recall one thing you said yes to recently. What did it cost you? (Time, energy, another task.) Write the hidden cost here.
If–Then: If I feel pressure to say "yes" to a request, then I will pause to consider the "hidden cost" before committing.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 6
fields.teaching_content: : Instead of a long to-do list, choose only 3 priorities each morning. If those 3 get done, the day is a win.
fields.practice_content:
: Write your Top 3 for tomorrow. Why these 3 and not others? Note your reasoning here.
If–Then: If I struggle to limit myself to 3 priorities, then I will ask which ones truly move the needle.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 7
fields.teaching_content: : You can’t prioritize well if you don’t know where your time actually goes. Small time leaks add up fast.
fields.practice_content:
: Track your time in 30-minute blocks today. At the end, note your biggest surprise about where time went.
If–Then: If I am surprised by where my time went, then I will adjust my schedule to protect one block for a high-value task.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 8
fields.teaching_content: : We often do easy, low-value tasks first because they feel productive. That’s comfort, not prioritizing.
fields.practice_content:
: Name one “comfort task” you default to (e.g., checking email, tidying). What important task does it delay? Write it here.
If–Then: If I catch myself defaulting to a "comfort task," then I will immediately switch to the important task it was delaying.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 9
fields.teaching_content: : Some tasks only you can do. Others could be done by anyone. Prioritize what requires your unique skills or judgment.
fields.practice_content:
: Look at your task list. Which items truly need you, and which could someone else handle? Mark them and note the difference.
If–Then: If I realize a task could be done by someone else, then I will note it for delegation rather than doing it myself.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 10
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve spent 10 days observing your priority habits. Awareness is the foundation for intentional choices.
fields.practice_content:
: On a 1–10 scale, how intentional are your daily priorities? What’s one pattern you’ve noticed? Log it here.
If–Then: If I find my intentionality score low, then I will pick one habit to change starting tomorrow.


Phase 2: Evaluating What Matters Most
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 11
fields.teaching_content: : Rate each task by impact: will it matter in a week? A month? A year? High-impact tasks deserve your best hours.
fields.practice_content:
: List 3 tasks. Rate each: matters this week only, this month, or this year. Move the longest-impact task to the top.
If–Then: If I see a task won't matter in a year, then I will deprioritize it in favor of long-impact work.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 12
fields.teaching_content: : Plot tasks on two axes: effort (high/low) and impact (high/low). Do high-impact, low-effort tasks first. That’s your sweet spot.
fields.practice_content:
: Take 4 tasks and place them in the matrix. Which is high-impact, low-effort? Do that one first tomorrow. Note it here.
If–Then: If I identify a high-impact, low-effort task, then I will schedule it to be done first.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 13
fields.teaching_content: : Roughly 20% of your tasks produce 80% of your results. Find that 20% and protect it fiercely.
fields.practice_content:
: Look at last week’s tasks. Which few produced the most meaningful results? Name them here—that’s your 20%.
If–Then: If I see I'm working outside my "20%," then I will streamline my list to focus on those high-result tasks.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 14
fields.teaching_content: : Your priorities don’t exist in a vacuum. Consider what matters to the people who depend on you or whom you depend on.
fields.practice_content:
: Name one key stakeholder (boss, partner, client). What’s their top priority right now? Does it align with yours? Note it.
If–Then: If I notice my priorities don't align with my key stakeholder, then I will schedule a brief check-in to realign.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 15
fields.teaching_content: : When two tasks seem equally important, your personal values break the tie. Know your values, and priorities get clearer.
fields.practice_content:
: Name your top 2 values (e.g., family, growth, health). Does your current task list reflect them? Write what you notice.
If–Then: If I face a tie between tasks, then I will choose the one that best reflects my top values.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 16
fields.teaching_content: : Ask: “If I don’t do this today, will I regret it tomorrow?” Regret cuts through noise and reveals what truly matters.
fields.practice_content:
: Apply the regret test to 3 tasks on your list. Which one would you most regret skipping? Move it up and note why.
If–Then: If I realize I will regret skipping a task, then I will move it to the top of my list for today.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 17
fields.teaching_content: : Not all deadlines are real. Some are arbitrary or self-imposed. Question every deadline before letting it drive your priorities.
fields.practice_content:
: Pick 3 upcoming deadlines. For each, ask: “Is this deadline real or flexible?” Note which ones you could renegotiate.
If–Then: If I see a deadline is flexible, then I will renegotiate it to prioritize more urgent work.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 18
fields.teaching_content: : A “not now” list is as powerful as a to-do list. It gives you permission to defer without forgetting.
fields.practice_content:
: Write 3 tasks you’re choosing NOT to prioritize this week. Put them on a “not now” list. How does it feel? Note it.
If–Then: If I feel the urge to do a task on my "not now" list, then I will remind myself why I deferred it.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 19
fields.teaching_content: : Priorities shift. A morning plan may not fit by noon. Build in a mid-day check: “Are my Top 3 still the right Top 3?”
fields.practice_content:
: At midday today, pause and re-evaluate your Top 3. Did anything change? What did you adjust? Write it here.
If–Then: If I see my Top 3 priorities no longer fit the day, then I will proactively adjust them.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 20
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve been learning to evaluate tasks by impact, effort, values, and real deadlines. Prioritizing is getting sharper.
fields.practice_content:
: Rate your ability to evaluate task importance 1–10. What’s one new filter you’re using? Log it here.
If–Then: If I find a specific filter useful, then I will integrate it into my daily planning routine.


Phase 3: Saying No and Setting Boundaries
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 21
fields.teaching_content: : Saying no to non-essential tasks is the most important prioritizing skill. It protects your time for what matters most.
fields.practice_content:
: Recall a recent time you said yes when you should have said no. What would you say instead now? Write your new response.
If–Then: If I feel the need to say "yes" out of habit, then I will use a "soft no" to protect my time.

fields.title: Day 22
fields.teaching_content: : You don’t have to say “no” bluntly. Try: “Not right now,” “I can do X but not Y,” or “Let me check my priorities first.”
fields.practice_content:
: Practice one soft no today on a low-stakes request. What phrase did you use? How did it go? Note it here.
If–Then: If I need to decline a request, then I will offer a clear "soft no" that protects our relationship.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 23
fields.teaching_content: : If your Top 3 priorities don’t have protected time, other people’s urgencies will always win. Block time for what matters.
fields.practice_content:
: Block 1 hour tomorrow for your #1 priority. Treat it like an unmovable meeting. Note when you scheduled it.
If–Then: If I see an interruption threatening my protected time, then I will reaffirm the boundary.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 24
fields.teaching_content: : Notifications, emails, and messages constantly rearrange your priorities. Set a boundary with one technology today.
fields.practice_content:
: Choose one tech boundary (e.g., no email before 10 AM, phone on silent for 1 hour). Try it today and note the result.
If–Then: If I feel overwhelmed by notifications, then I will turn off one tech trigger during my priority time.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 25
fields.teaching_content: : If someone else can do it 70% as well, delegate it. Your time is better spent on tasks only you can do.

: Name one task you could delegate this week. Who could do it? What would you do with the freed time? Write it here.
If–Then: If I find a task I could delegate, then I will write down the instructions to hand it off today.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.teaching_content: : Guilt after saying no is normal but misleading. It doesn’t mean you made the wrong choice—it means you’re not used to it yet.

: If you said no to something recently and felt guilty, write what you protected by saying no. Was it worth it?
If–Then: If I feel guilty after saying no, then I will revisit what I protected by saying no.

fields.teaching_content: : Not every urgent request from others is your emergency. Ask: “Is this truly urgent, or does it just feel urgent to them?”

: Recall a recent “urgent” request from someone. Was it genuinely urgent for you? What would happen if you delayed 24 hours? Note it.

fields.title: Day 30
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve been practicing boundaries and saying no. These are the muscles that make prioritizing sustainable.

: Rate your comfort saying no to non-essential tasks 1–10. What’s one boundary you’re proud of? Log it here.

Phase 4: Energy Management and Timing

fields.title: Day 31
fields.teaching_content: : Prioritizing isn’t just about time—it’s about energy. Do your hardest priorities when your energy is highest.
fields.practice_content:
: Track your energy today: when were you sharpest? Schedule your #1 priority there tomorrow. Note your energy peak.
If–Then: If I feel my energy dipping, then I will schedule my next high-priority task when I am at my peak.

fields.title: Day 32
fields.teaching_content: : Every decision drains your battery. Reduce small decisions (what to wear, what to eat) to save energy for big priorities.
fields.practice_content:
: Name 2 small daily decisions you could automate or pre-decide. Try one tomorrow and note the effect on your focus.
If–Then: If I find myself drained by small decisions, then I will automate one of them for tomorrow.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 33
fields.teaching_content: : If a task takes under 2 minutes, do it immediately—it costs more energy to track it than to finish it.

: Notice 3 tiny tasks today and do them immediately. Did clearing them free mental space for bigger priorities? Note it.
If–Then: If a task takes less than 2 minutes, then I will do it immediately instead of adding it to my list.

fields.title: Day 34
fields.teaching_content: : Group low-energy tasks (admin, errands, easy emails) into one block during your low-energy period. Don’t scatter them.
fields.practice_content:
: Identify your low-energy window today. Batch 3–5 small tasks there. How did it feel vs. scattering them? Write it here.
If–Then: If I have a low-energy period, then I will batch my administrative tasks to maximize my capacity.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 35
fields.teaching_content: : Rest isn’t laziness—it’s fuel. If you don’t prioritize recovery, your other priorities will suffer from diminished energy.
fields.practice_content:
: Schedule one intentional recovery block tomorrow (walk, nap, break). Treat it as a real priority. Note what you chose.
If–Then: If I feel depleted, then I will prioritize an intentional recovery block.

fields.title: Day 36
fields.teaching_content: : Sometimes the hardest no is to your own impulse—the urge to check social media, start a new project, or chase a shiny idea.

: Name one impulse that regularly hijacks your priorities. What’s your plan to say no to it today? Write it here.
If–Then: If I feel an impulse to check distractions, then I will label it and commit to focusing on my priority.

fields.teaching_content: : Instead of working on priorities all day, try 90-minute focused sprints with breaks. Intensity beats duration.

fields.teaching_content: : Every time you switch tasks, your brain takes 15–25 minutes to fully re-engage. Minimize switching to protect priorities.

: Count how many times you switched tasks today. What triggered each switch? Note one switch you could have avoided.

fields.title: Day 39
fields.teaching_content: : Spending 5 minutes at day’s end to set tomorrow’s priorities means you start the next day with clarity, not scrambling.

If–Then: If I am tempted to end my day without planning, then I will force myself to write down my Top 3 for tomorrow.

fields.title: Day 40
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve learned to align priorities with energy, reduce decision fatigue, and use sprints. Prioritizing is now strategic.

: Rate your energy management around priorities 1–10. What’s one strategy that’s making the biggest difference? Log it.
If–Then: If I find my energy management inconsistent, then I will tighten my alignment of tasks and peak times.


Phase 5: Prioritizing Under Pressure

fields.title: Day 41
fields.teaching_content: : When everything feels urgent, stop and ask: “What is the one thing that, if done, makes everything else easier or unnecessary?”
fields.practice_content:
: Think of a time you felt overwhelmed. Apply the “one thing” question. What surfaces as the true priority? Write it.
If–Then: If I feel overwhelmed, then I will ask "what is the one thing?" to narrow my focus.

fields.title: Day 42
fields.teaching_content: : In a crisis, use triage: what must happen now, what can wait an hour, what can wait a day? Sort ruthlessly, act sequentially.
fields.practice_content:
: Imagine 5 tasks all hit at once. Sort them into: now, within an hour, can wait. Write your triage and your reasoning.
If–Then: If I face a sudden crisis, then I will triage my tasks and act on the highest-priority item first.

fields.title: Day 43
fields.teaching_content: : When two people need you urgently, clarify impact and timeline with each. Transparency buys goodwill and time.
fields.practice_content:
: Recall a time two demands collided. How did you choose? What would you do differently now? Write your approach.
If–Then: If I have competing demands, then I will communicate the conflict and clarify expectations.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 44
fields.teaching_content: : Shared priorities need shared agreement. A team that isn’t aligned on what matters wastes everyone’s effort.
fields.practice_content:
: If you work with others, ask one person: “What’s your #1 priority this week?” Compare it to yours. Note the alignment.
If–Then: If I see team misalignment, then I will ask for clarity on our #1 priority.
fields.reflection_question: How did today's practice make you feel?

fields.title: Day 45
fields.teaching_content: : If everything is high priority, nothing is. Push back: force-rank your list even when it’s uncomfortable. Someone has to choose.

: Take your current task list and force-rank every item. No ties allowed. What did ranking reveal? Write your top 5.
If–Then: If I feel everything is high priority, then I will force-rank my list to reveal the true essential.

fields.title: Day 46
fields.teaching_content: : Tasks aren’t the only thing to prioritize. Relationships need intentional time too, or they erode under busyness.

: Name one relationship you’ve been neglecting because of tasks. Schedule 15 minutes for that person this week. Note who.
If–Then: If I see I'm neglecting a relationship, then I will schedule 15 minutes of dedicated time.

fields.teaching_content: : Short-term priorities feel urgent. Long-term priorities build your future. Spend at least 20% of your time on long-term.

: What’s one long-term priority you keep deferring? Give it 20 minutes today. What did you do? Log it here.
If–Then: If I keep deferring a long-term goal, then I will dedicate 20 minutes to it today.

fields.title: Day 48
fields.teaching_content: : Each week, reset: what were my priorities, what actually happened, and what should next week’s priorities be?

: Do a weekly reset now. Write last week’s intended vs. actual priorities, and next week’s Top 3. Note the gaps.
If–Then: If I notice a gap in my weekly reset, then I will adjust next week's plan immediately.

fields.title: Day 49
fields.teaching_content: : You can’t prioritize well when you’re depleted. Sleep, exercise, and mental health aren’t optional—they’re foundational.

: Rate how well you’ve prioritized self-care this week (1–10). Name one self-care action you’ll protect next week.
If–Then: If I feel my self-care sliding, then I will protect one non-negotiable health habit.

fields.title: Day 50
fields.teaching_content: : You’ve practiced prioritizing under pressure, with teams, and across time horizons. This is advanced prioritizing.

: Rate your overall prioritizing skill 1–10. What’s the biggest shift in how you manage competing demands? Log it.

Phase 6: Integration and Identity

fields.teaching_content: : By now you have tools: Top 3, impact filter, soft no, sprints, triage. Name the system that works for you.
